data.title: Credentials and Internal Detail in Published Documents
data.summary: Documents published on public sites and third-party platforms contained internal hostnames, architecture detail and, in places, working credentials — in screenshots, appendices and presenter notes as well as in the body text.
data.description:
Documents leak through the parts nobody re-reads. A screenshot in a case study shows a populated interface, including hostnames and sometimes a token in a URL. A conference deck carries presenter notes and an architecture diagram with real addresses. A tender response includes an appendix listing systems and versions.

Credentials appear more often than expected, usually as examples that happen to be real: an API key in a sample request, a test account that still works, a connection string in a configuration appendix.

Third-party platforms widen the exposure — slide-sharing sites, support forums and partner portals host copies long after the original is withdrawn.
data.recommendation:
* Review documents for internal detail before publication, including screenshots, notes and appendices.
* Treat any credential that has appeared in a document as compromised and rotate it.
* Keep a register of what has been published externally, so it can be reviewed when a system changes.
* Search for your own material on third-party platforms periodically.
data.short_recommendation: Review documents for internal detail before publishing, and rotate what leaked.
